records.title: The Midnight Ghost Bus Route 375 of Beijing
records.summary: A legendary staple of modern Chinese internet creepypasta and urban folklore, Route 375 (or 330) involves the final midnight bus departing the Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan) terminal toward the Fragrant Hills on November 14, 1995. Late along the route, the driver picked up two men in Qing Dynasty robes supporting a third man whose head was slumped forward. An observant old woman passenger noticed that when a breeze stirred the men's long robes, they had no feet and were hovering above the floorboards. Faking a theft to drag a young man off the bus at the next stop, she saved his life: the following morning, the bus was recovered submerged in a reservoir sixteen kilometers away, with decaying corpses and fuel tanks filled with fresh blood.
alternate_names: The Midnight Bus to Fragrant Hills
records.historical_period: November 1995 to Present (viral BBS netlore since late 1990s)

records.title: The Spectral Concubines of the Forbidden City
records.summary: The vast imperial Forbidden City in Beijing, home to twenty-four Ming and Qing dynasty emperors, was the site of numerous palace intrigues, poisonings, and executions of imperial concubines and eunuchs. A widely circulated Beijing urban legend asserts that nocturnal security guards on the 5:00 PM closing shift encounter court maidens and concubines dressed in elaborate Qing Dynasty silk robes and high manchu headpieces walking along the narrow red-walled corridors in the moonlight. During summer thunderstorms, visitors report lightning flashes revealing the projected shadows of imperial maidens playing flutes along the palace walls, attributed to iron oxide in the ancient vermilion plaster.
alternate_names: The Ghosts of the Forbidden City
The Palace Maidens of the Vermilion Walls
records.historical_period: Ming/Qing dynasties to Modern Urban Folklore

records.title: The Braemar Hill Ghost Girl of Hong Kong
records.summary: Surrounded by prestigious secondary schools and luxury residential complexes on Hong Kong Island, Braemar Hill is the focal point of persistent school ghostlore. Following a tragic double murder in the wooded reservoir in 1985, students walking up Cloud View Road late in the afternoon report encounters with a pale teenage schoolgirl in a British colonial school uniform who stands motionless in the mountain mist. Motorists driving along the dark curves have reported the girl stepping into the road, causing cars to brake violently only for the figure to dissipate like steam over the harbor.

records.title: The Lotus Pond Drowned Maiden
records.summary: A widely documented Chinese university campus legend centers on serene lotus ponds located across major collegiate grounds, notably National Taiwan University and Tsinghua University. According to the legend, an earnest female student drowned herself in the lotus pond at midnight after being betrayed by her lover. At midnight, solitary students walking across the decorative arched stone bridges report being approached by a weeping maiden with her hair draped forward who asks: 'Excuse me, what time is it?' Looking down, the listener sees her dress is soaking wet with pond water and weed; answering her directly causes her to drag the student into the dark water.
alternate_names: The Midnight Question of the Lotus Pond
records.historical_period: Late 20th Century University Era (c. 1970s to present)

records.title: The Haunted Caoxi Road Metro Station in Shanghai
records.summary: Located on Shanghai Metro Line 3, Caoxi Road Station was constructed over an area that historically served as an execution ground and a mass burial site during the early 20th century. Metro maintenance engineers and late-night station sweepers report uncanny occurrences after the last train departs: disembodied footsteps running along empty platforms, automated turnstiles clicking rapidly as if invisible throngs are passing through, and phantom shadows gliding across track cameras in the darkened tunnels, inspiring widespread caution among nocturnal commuters.

records.title: The Xiangxi Corpse-Walking Sorcerers (Xiangxi Gan Shi)
records.summary: Deep in the misty karst mountains of western Hunan (Xiangxi) among the Miao and Tujia ethnic communities, the practice of Xiangxi Gan Shi ('Driving Corpses in Western Hunan') is one of China's most chilling folk traditions. Taoist necromancers (Zhuayoushi) performed nocturnal rituals to transport the corpses of migrant laborers who died far from home back to their ancestral villages for burial. Moving strictly at night along secluded mountain trails, the sorcerer rang a brass bell, chanted incantations, and burned yellow paper talismans while a line of rigid corpses bound in white robes hopped synchronously behind him.
alternate_names: The Hopping Dead of Western Hunan
records.historical_period: Qing Dynasty to Early 20th Century (sustained in modern folklore)

records.title: The Cursed Chaonei No. 81 Mansion in Beijing
records.summary: Situated at 81 Chaoyangmennei Street in central Beijing, this decaying three-story French Baroque brick mansion has stood abandoned behind twisted ivy for decades. According to widely circulated urban legend, during the fall of the Kuomintang government in 1949, a high-ranking Nationalist officer abandoned his concubine in the house as he fled to Taiwan; in despair, the woman hanged herself from the rafters. For decades, urban explorers have reported unexplainable temperature drops, disembodied weeping during summer storms, and light anomalies, earning the building the title of 'The Most Haunted House in Beijing.'
alternate_names: The French Baroque Ghost House of Beijing

records.title: The Ghost Bride Market of Fengjie (Minghun)
records.summary: Rooted in ancient Chinese beliefs that an unmarried youth who dies without a spouse will wander the afterlife as an envious, lonely hungry ghost, the practice of Minghun ('Ghost Marriage' or posthumous wedding) has persisted in rural provinces like Shanxi and Shaanxi. While traditionally conducted between deceased families who interred matching clay effigies, 20th-century urban legends and criminal investigations revealed illicit underworld black markets where body-snatchers dug up female cadavers to sell to bereaved families for exorbitant prices, cementing modern horror regarding nocturnal cemetery pillaging.
records.historical_period: Imperial era to 20th/21st Century criminal cases and folklore
records.region_or_community: Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Henan rural districts

records.title: The Whispering Pagoda of Hangzhou West Lake (Leifeng)
records.summary: Crowning Sunset Hill along the southern banks of West Lake in Hangzhou, the ancient Leifeng Pagoda was originally erected in 975 CE. Following its catastrophic structural collapse in September 1924, local superstitions claimed that the magical brick dust of the pagoda cured illnesses and protected homes from snakes. Modern urban legend claims that when the pagoda was rebuilt in bronze and glass in 2002 over the preserved stone ruins, subterranean acoustic phenomena caused visitors descending into the archaeological foundation chamber to hear the rhythmic hissing and whispering of Bai Suzhen, the White Snake spirit.
records.historical_period: 1924 collapse to 2002 reconstruction and living urban lore

records.title: The Dragon King Mountain Ghost Cavern of Zhejiang
records.summary: Located in the Anji bamboo forests of Zhejiang Province, Dragon King Mountain (Longwang Shan) is the headwaters of the Huangpu River that flows through Shanghai. Local mountaineers and bamboo harvesters recount urban legends of deep limestone sinkholes and caverns that emit sudden rushing gales and low droning rumbles resembling a sleeping dragon's respiration. Nocturnal campers report seeing jade-green luminous lights hovering above the bamboo canopy, accompanied by sudden electronic compass failures and phantom voices calling hikers deeper into the mist-shrouded limestone gorges.
